did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with the heading “For the music director, with stringed instruments; a maskil of David,” indicating that it was meant to be performed with music and is called a “maskil.”
The psalmist describes his distress in both body and soul: his heart “writhes within him,” and the terrors of death fall upon him.
To express his desire to escape the danger, the psalmist uses the image of a dove: “If only I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest.”
The city described in the psalm is not a place of safety: violence, strife, wrongdoing, and trouble surround it, and the psalmist asks the Lord to confuse the tongues of the wicked.
The deepest pain comes when it becomes clear that the offender is not a distant enemy, but someone who had been close to the psalmist—his companion and trusted friend.
The closeness between the psalmist and the person who betrayed him is also described as spiritual fellowship: together they shared intimate counsel and went to the house of God in deep companionship.
The psalmist mentions three times of prayer each day—evening, morning, and noon—and emphasizes that prayer is an ongoing practice, not a one-time act.
The psalm contrasts outward appearance with inner reality: the traitor’s words are smooth and gentle like oil, but there is war in his heart.
At the heart of the conclusion is a call to cast one’s “burden” or worry upon the Lord, trusting that he will sustain the person and never let the righteous be shaken.
The final verse sets the fate of deceitful and violent people, who go down to the pit of destruction, against the psalmist’s stance: “But I will trust in you.”
